title: Whitney Embedding Tubular Neighbourhoods and Approximation

items.title: A finite coordinate-bump map embeds a compact manifold in some Euclidean space
items.strategy: Choose a finite regular chart cover, multiply each coordinate map by a bump that is identically one on a smaller core, and append the bump scalars themselves. Equality in one active chart forces equality of points, and compactness upgrades the resulting injective immersion to an embedding.

items.title: A countable coordinate-bump map embeds a manifold in countable Euclidean data
items.strategy: Take a countable relatively compact coordinate-ball cover, attach one compactly supported coordinate block to each chart, and append the scalar support functions. Local finiteness makes the map smooth and the scalar blocks remember which charts are active, so the map is an injective immersion into countably many Euclidean coordinates.

items.title: A smooth exhaustion separates the locally finite chart bands
items.strategy: Use a smooth proper exhaustion to cut the manifold into overlapping compact bands, then choose finitely many coordinate-bump blocks on each band with disjoint same-parity supports and geometric-series bounds.

items.title: Every smooth manifold embeds in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space
items.strategy: Use the finite coordinate-bump construction in the compact case and the standard noncompact Whitney construction to obtain an embedding of the form p |-> (G(p), rho(p)) with G bounded and rho proper.

items.title: A proper injective immersion is a smooth embedding
items.strategy: An immersion is locally an embedding. Properness makes the underlying continuous map closed between locally compact Hausdorff spaces, so the corestriction to its image is a homeomorphism and the local embedded-submanifold charts patch to a global smooth embedding.

items.title: Secant and tangent direction maps of a Euclidean embedding
A generic linear projection preserves injectivity and immersion
items.strategy: Bad projection directions are exactly the secant directions that identify two points and the tangent directions that kill a nonzero tangent vector. Both bad sets are images of lower-dimensional smooth manifolds, hence null, so their complement is dense and any direction there gives an injective immersion after projection.

items.title: A generic projection can preserve properness
items.strategy: For an embedding F=(g,rho) with g bounded and rho proper, choose a projection direction with nonzero rho-component and outside the secant and tangent bad sets; the projected map remains proper because bounded target balls force bounded rho-values.

items.title: The weak Whitney proper embedding theorem
items.strategy: Start from a finite-dimensional embedding, promote it to a proper embedding with an added proper coordinate, and then project one dimension at a time while avoiding the secant, tangent, and properness-breaking directions. Iteration stops in dimension 2n+1 and still yields a proper embedding.

items.title: The weak Whitney immersion theorem
items.strategy: Invoke the classical Whitney immersion theorem, which places every smooth n-manifold in R^{2n}.

items.title: The strong Whitney embedding theorem
The strong Whitney immersion theorem
Tubular neighbourhoods of embedded submanifolds
The normal addition map for a Euclidean submanifold
Normal addition is a local diffeomorphism along the zero section
items.strategy: Along the zero section the differential of normal addition sends the tangent directions to the tangent space of the submanifold and the normal directions to the ambient normal space. These two summands span the ambient tangent space, so the inverse function theorem gives local diffeomorphism along the zero section.

items.title: Variable-radius injectivity for normal addition
items.strategy: For each base point, take the maximal local-diffeomorphism radius of normal addition, prove that radius varies continuously, smooth a positive minorant, and then use the half-radius estimate to force any two coincident images into one injective local chart.

items.title: The Euclidean tubular neighbourhood theorem
items.strategy: Invoke the classical Euclidean tubular-neighbourhood theorem for the normal addition map of an embedded Euclidean submanifold.

items.title: A closed Euclidean submanifold has a smooth neighborhood retraction
items.strategy: Invert the tubular chart and project each normal vector to its base point. Composing with the tubular diffeomorphism yields a smooth retraction from the tube onto the submanifold.

items.title: Nearest-point projection is the tubular retraction after shrinking
items.strategy: On a sufficiently small tube, the squared distance to the submanifold is minimized exactly at the base point of the normal fiber. For compact submanifolds one may choose a uniform radius; in general only a variable radius is available.

items.title: The tubular neighbourhood theorem in a smooth ambient manifold
items.strategy: Invoke the classical tubular-neighbourhood theorem for closed embedded submanifolds of smooth ambient manifolds, interpreted through the library's normal-bundle definition.

items.title: Every closed embedded submanifold has a smooth neighborhood retraction
items.strategy: A tubular neighborhood comes with a bundle projection to the zero section. Transferring that projection through the tubular diffeomorphism gives the ambient smooth retraction.

items.title: Two tubular neighbourhood germs are isomorphic near the zero section
items.strategy: Compose one tubular chart with the inverse of the other. This composite fixes the zero section and has identity differential there, so after shrinking both tubes it becomes the desired vector-bundle-side isomorphism of germs.

items.title: Positive continuous error functions for strong approximation
Whitney approximation for Euclidean-valued maps
items.strategy: Choose a countable locally finite cover on which the continuous map varies less than the prescribed local error, replace it locally by constants, and glue those local models with a smooth partition of unity. The error estimate is carried pointwise by the convex combination.

items.title: Relative Whitney approximation for Euclidean-valued maps
items.strategy: Extend the already smooth restriction on a neighborhood of the closed set, leave that extension untouched on a smaller neighborhood, and apply the Euclidean approximation theorem only on the complement. A cutoff supported away from the fixed region glues the two pieces without changing the map near the closed set.

items.title: A fine Euclidean approximation lands in a prescribed tubular neighbourhood
items.strategy: Pull the available tube radius back along the original map and choose the approximation error pointwise smaller than that radius. The approximating Euclidean map then stays inside the tubular neighborhood everywhere.

items.title: Whitney approximation for manifold-valued maps
items.strategy: Embed the target manifold in Euclidean space, approximate the composite map there, and choose the Euclidean approximation fine enough to stay inside a tubular neighborhood of the embedded target. Retracting through that tube yields a smooth map, and the straight segment inside the tube followed by retraction gives the homotopy to the original map.

items.title: Relative Whitney approximation for manifold-valued maps
items.strategy: Use the relative Euclidean approximation theorem after embedding the target, then retract through the same tubular neighborhood as in the absolute theorem. Because the Euclidean approximation agrees with the original map near the chosen closed set, the retracted map does too.

items.title: Every continuous map between smooth manifolds is homotopic to a smooth map
items.strategy: Apply the manifold-valued Whitney approximation theorem and retain the homotopy it constructs through the tubular neighborhood.

items.title: Continuously homotopic smooth maps are smoothly homotopic
items.strategy: View a continuous homotopy as a continuous map on M times I, reparameterize it to be constant on endpoint collars, extend it constantly to M times R, and apply the relative manifold-valued approximation theorem fixing the two collar regions. Restricting back to M times I gives a smooth homotopy between the original smooth endpoint maps.

items.title: The smooth and continuous homotopy categories of smooth manifolds have the same morphism sets
items.strategy: One corollary replaces each continuous map by a smooth homotopic representative, and the smoothing-of-homotopies theorem shows this representative is unique up to smooth homotopy whenever the original continuous maps were homotopic.

items.title: A continuous map from a closed subset extends smoothly exactly when it has a continuous extension and is smooth near the subset
items.strategy: The only nontrivial direction is to start from a continuous extension that is already smooth near the closed subset and apply the relative manifold-valued approximation theorem to smooth the rest without changing the map near that subset.

items.title: A tubular target produces a submersive finite-dimensional perturbation family
items.strategy: Use the standard finite-dimensional perturbation family around a smooth map into a manifold; each pointwise parameter map is a submersion, so the evaluation map is a submersion and therefore transverse to every embedded target submanifold.

items.title: The transversality homotopy theorem
items.strategy: Choose a global finite-dimensional perturbation family with submersive evaluation map, apply parametric transversality to get a transverse slice, and connect it to the original map by the straight parameter homotopy inside the open parameter ball.

items.title: Strong Whitney approximation by transverse maps
items.strategy: Use the standard strong-topology transversality theorem: every strong neighbourhood of a smooth map contains a transverse smooth map.

items.title: Transverse maps are dense in the strong smooth topology
items.strategy: Apply the strong Whitney approximation theorem with any positive locally finite strong-topology error control.

items.title: A smooth section transverse to the zero section has a submanifold zero set
items.strategy: Reinterpret transversality to the zero section as surjectivity of the vertical differential at each zero, then apply the zero-set proposition for transverse sections.

items.title: Relative transversality preserves a map on a closed good region
items.strategy: Insert a squared cutoff into the global perturbation family so the parameter and its first derivative vanish on the protected region, keep the evaluation map transverse there, and then choose a transverse slice by parametric transversality.

items.title: FALSE: every injective immersion is a proper embedding
items.strategy: Refute the claim with an injective immersion whose image accumulates topologically or whose inverse image of a compact set is noncompact. The proposition on proper injective immersions gives the exact extra hypothesis that is missing.

items.title: FALSE: an arbitrary linear projection of an embedding is an embedding
items.strategy: Refute by projecting an embedded submanifold along a bad secant or bad tangent direction. The generic-projection lemma identifies exactly which directions must be excluded.

items.title: FALSE: every proper embedding of an n-manifold lands in R^n
items.strategy: If such an embedding existed in full dimension, invariance-of-domain behavior would force an open image and local diffeomorphism features that fail for many manifolds. The weak Whitney theorem gives the honest ambient dimension guarantee instead.

items.title: FALSE: every noncompact submanifold has a uniform-radius tubular neighbourhood
items.strategy: Refute by an embedded submanifold whose distinct ends approach each other with reach tending to zero. The Euclidean tubular theorem only promises a variable radius in general, and that dependence is genuine.

items.title: FALSE: the tubular-neighbourhood retraction is canonical
items.strategy: Different choices of tube or metric yield different retractions even though their germs agree near the zero section after shrinking. The germ-isomorphism proposition records the right uniqueness statement and no stronger one.

items.title: FALSE: uniform approximation is the right global notion on every noncompact manifold
items.strategy: Refute with a noncompact source or target where one global epsilon cannot control approximation near infinity. The Euclidean Whitney theorem uses a positive continuous error function precisely because point-dependent control is the honest global notion.

title: Whitney Embedding Tubular Neighbourhoods and Approximation — Examples

items.title: The standard circle and its annular tubular neighbourhood
items.strategy: Write the normal addition map for S^1 inside R^2 explicitly, identify its image as a thin annulus, and compute the retraction by radial normalization.

items.title: The sphere and its two-sided normal tube
items.strategy: Use the outward unit normal field on the sphere to identify the normal line bundle explicitly and then describe the corresponding spherical shell tubular neighborhood.

items.title: A noncompact embedded curve with no uniform tubular radius
items.strategy: Build a smooth curve with parallel hairpin branches approaching each other at infinity. Local embeddedness is clear, but any fixed tube radius eventually meets both branches and destroys injectivity of the normal exponential picture.

items.title: A coordinate-bump embedding of the circle in Euclidean space
items.strategy: Choose a two-chart cover of the circle, attach the compactly supported coordinate blocks from the compact embedding proof, and write the resulting explicit map into Euclidean space.

items.title: Projecting a space curve can create a double point
items.strategy: Take a simple embedded space curve and project it along a visibly bad secant direction so that two distinct points collapse in the plane.

items.title: Smoothing a piecewise-linear real-valued function relative to a closed set
items.strategy: Keep the function fixed on a closed neighborhood where it is already smooth and smooth only the remaining corners by the relative Whitney approximation theorem.

items.title: Smoothing a continuous circle-valued map through an annular retraction
items.strategy: Embed the circle in the plane, approximate the continuous planar representative, and retract the approximation back to the circle through the standard annular tubular neighborhood.

items.title: A generic section of a line bundle has a hypersurface zero set
items.strategy: Apply the transverse-section corollary to a line bundle and note that transversality to the zero section forces the zero set to have codimension one.

items.title: A nearest-point projection need not be unique outside the tubular radius
items.strategy: For the unit circle, the center of the circle is equidistant from every point of the circle, so nearest-point projection is not uniquely defined once one leaves the small annular tube.

items.title: A smooth approximation without relative control destroys prescribed values
items.strategy: Exhibit a continuous map that is already smooth on a closed set and approximate it smoothly without imposing the relative condition; the new map moves the previously fixed values, showing why the relative theorem is genuinely stronger.
